body: Mozilla would be interested in implementing this, but can't give you an ETA.

I will implement this in Blink behind a flag to get feedback from developers.

Adding any property to document is fraught because it can shadow bindings on the global in inline event handlers. We'll try to gather feedback if not data on that.
@dominiccooney good point, why not just mark them `[Unscopable]` from the get go?
Great! I'll mark them [Unscopeable], and with two implementers in support, I'll start writing tests next week.

I'm not certain I like the idea of adding three new attributes on `document`.  How about something like `document.whenReady('interactive')`?  I'm particularly concerned about `document.interactive` because that seems like the name we can use for something else.

Some more discussion in #whatwg at http://logs.glob.uno/?c=freenode%23whatwg&s=31%20Oct%202016&e=31%20Oct%202016#c1010329 with @rniwa. It emerged that he's mostly concerned about `document.interactive` using up a name that we might want in the future for a hypothetical "Interactive API". The other two he's not as concerned with.

So if we can come up with an alternate name that would help. Some suggestions were `interactiveReady`, `interactionReady`, `readyToInteractive`.

But apart from that, @rniwa is indifferent to the API, so we shouldn't really take this as a sign of support.

How about a common prefix for these (nice for autocomplete etc), like:
- `whenInteractive`
- `whenContentLoaded`
- `whenLoaded`
We haven't done that for other promise-returning properties, and it hurts usability. Worth considering though.
Tests up at https://github.com/w3c/web-platform-tests/pull/4171. [Unscopable] added. Ready for editor review.

I'm a bit confused by the document.open handling here.  Say I have a DOMContentLoaded event listener which calls document.open().  What will the state of the various promises involved be after https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-end step 4?  As far as I can tell, the document will be in the "loading" state but its "content loaded promise" will be resolved...

Ah, yes, I thought that the order between events and promise operations did not matter due to microtask handling, but you're right and have found a case where it does. I think the fix is to resolve the promise first there, before firing the event. Then if firing the event causes it (and the others) to reset to a new promise via `document.open`, nothing bad happens.

Will fix and add such a test case.

Briefly discussed this with @jakearchibald and he didn't feel it would cause too much confusion, but adding a note for reference: 

When speaking to developers about `document.interactive` their first gut instinct has been that this refers to a moment during load when the document is actually interactive (layout has stabilized and the main thread is available enough to handle user input as most scripts have settled). Not when `readyState` becomes `interactive`. This definition of interactivity is closer to the WebPerf notion of "time to interactivity" as covered by something like https://github.com/tdresser/time-to-interactive (cc @tdresser).

I think loading states as promises add value to the platform, but am concerned about the confusion the `interactive` wording might have. `readyState` already had a notion of `interactive` prior to "time to interactive" being cared about as a metric in webdev circles, so if others don't have this concern that's fine. I know `{interactive, loaded}` are pretty terse and are also attractive in that regard.
Do you have an alternative term?
How about `document.contentLoaded`?

@rniwa that's taken (the promise for `DOMContentLoaded`). 😊

Do web developers know when `readyState` changes to `interactive`? Looking at github search it appears it is not uncommon to assume it is when `DOMContentLoaded` fires. It's not clear to me that it is the best option to use the terminology of `document.readyState`.

The `contentLoaded` and `loaded` promises use wording for events rather than `document.readyState`, and nobody complains about these, right?

In https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/127#issuecomment-254931526 `document.parsed` was suggested as a possible name. While it doesn't match up with `document.readyState`, I think it is probably closer to what most people will think it does. Explaining it would be along the lines of "`document.parsed` resolves when the document is parsed, before deferred and async scripts have run. `document.readyState` is changed to `interactive` at the same time."

@zcorpan very few developers know this stuff. I made it a question at Chrome Dev Summit https://youtu.be/aWGU4qLtHEw?t=1h40m28s

When asked "What comes first? `document.onload`, `readyState == 'interactive'`, or `DOMContentLoaded`?" here were the results:

* 40% said `document.onload`
* 40% said `DOMContentLoaded`
* 20% said `readyState == 'interactive'`

Btw I like the general rule of following event names for equivalent promises, but given developer confusion around this, and @rniwa's concerns (although I don't share them), `document.parsed` feels much better.

> `document.parsed` was suggested as a possible name. While it doesn't match up with document.readyState, I think it is probably closer to what most people will think it does. 

I agree with @jakearchibald that `document.parsed` does feel better and would help minimize confusion.
I'll switch the tests and spec to document.parsed then. Thanks for the feedback all!

So from the web-platform-tests PR the reason this has not moved forward is because implementers have not moved towards implementing. Sometimes that happens because they are waiting for the standard to change.

Pinging @dominiccooney @cdumez @rniwa @bzbarsky @smaug---- @travisleithead once again to make sure we didn't deadlock ourselves since this all seems ready to go and lots of web developers have expressed support.

I'm having second thoughts about this. Do we really need to have both `document.parsed` and `document.contentLoaded`? Put it another way, do authors really differentiate `document.readyState == 'interactive'` and `DOMContentLoaded` in practice?

For example, [a MDN article on `readyState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/readyState) mentions <q>readystatechange as an alternative to DOMContentLoaded event</q>. That seems to suggest that these two things are more or less interchangeable for many authors. In fact, I myself don't really care the difference between these two things when I'm writing an Web app.

It might be actually better to have just either one of `contentLoaded` or `parsed` whichever fits authors' mental model better. We might also want to take a look at the broader picture of how a typical modern Web app loads, and how each milestone such as HTML/XML parser completing, deferred scrips running, the first non-black paint happening, etc... fit together.

For example, [navigation timing 2](https://w3c.github.io/navigation-timing/#sec-PerformanceNavigationTiming) has `domContentLoadedEventStart` and `domContentLoadedEventEnd` on [`PerformanceNavigationTiming`](https://w3c.github.io/navigation-timing/#dom-performancenavigationtiming). Presumably these two properties exist to measure the amount of time the app spent initializing itself during `DOMContentLoaded`. Adding `document.contentLoaded` could break this API depending on when it's resolved because now scripts are doing more work at the end of the microtask after `DOMContentLoaded` had fired. In fact, the current PR doesn't make it clear whether this promise is resolved before the event is fired or after the event is fired. Given the aforementioned properties on the navigation timing 2, it's imperative that we define this.

> I'm having second thoughts about this. Do we really need to have both document.parsed and document.contentLoaded? Put it another way, do authors really differentiate document.readyState == 'interactive' and DOMContentLoaded in practice?

That's definitely a good question.

The reason I included contentLoaded is because it's so widely used by authors, e.g. via jQuery (where it is called `$.ready`) or just manually. I think in many cases authors would have been better off using document.readyState === 'interactive' ("parsed") timing, since it's sooner, but I didn't want to second-guess them. And I didn't see many drawbacks to exposing all three, especially if this is part of a larger pattern of exposing one-time events as promises. We can provide authors the tools and let them use them appropriately.

> In fact, the current PR doesn't make it clear whether this promise is resolved before the event is fired or after the event is fired. Given the aforementioned properties on the navigation timing 2, it's imperative that we define this.

This is very well-defined by the current spec PR. Lines 108153-108156 which resolve the promise are before lines 108157-108160 that fire the event. What do you find ambiguous about this?

That means though that the event listeners run first and then any promise callbacks at the end of that task (before any promises resolved by the event listeners).

As is tradition in the Web Performance Working Group they have unfortunately not even monkey patched algorithms let alone filed bugs for hooks, so how exactly their timestamps relate to any promises (new or those resolved in event listeners that run at the end of that task) is completely unclear. I filed https://github.com/w3c/navigation-timing/issues/63, but I don't think that should block this PR, since as I demonstrated it's already vague.

Hey there, I was curious about the state of this feature.

> it's just missing any implementer actually prioritizing it highly enough.
> — @domenic [Feb 6](https://github.com/whatwg/dom/issues/568#issuecomment-363633336)

That comment is from a related issue, but is that the reason this PR has been on hold? I’d just like to understand, and I’m sorry if I missed any unresolved issues that came up in other discussions.
Yes, that's the reason.

When the `document.readyState` is called `complete`, then why not use `completelyLoaded`

It's hard to know which one of `loaded` or `contentLoaded` is most complete without knowing the existing events

> I'm having second thoughts about this. Do we really need to have both document.parsed and document.contentLoaded? Put it another way, do authors really differentiate document.readyState == 'interactive' and DOMContentLoaded in practice?

@rniwa,
The answer is, absolutely yes! Or authors sadly don't, when they *should*. It's in fact critical for performance and how every Ad should be loaded. The former is for modifying the DOM before the browser starts painting. The latter manipulates a DOM that already started painting.

Injecting all things in a `<body>` on DOMContentLoaded is a poor visual experience and incur unnecessary re-renders and repaints.

e.g. I modify or hide an element before first paint, and show it again once modified as a fade-in. I have been doing this for `mailto:` obfuscated email links, and images only once verified that they are loaded, while also predetermining and injecting the height of img's element on interactive (to avoid any position shift while painting the document). I hide those element on 'interactive' and only start showing them or triggering a fade at/after DOMContentLoaded.

> The former is for modifying the DOM before the browser starts painting. The latter manipulates a DOM that already started painting.

Painting can happen before either.

> Painting can happen before either.

Only on Chrome AFAICT where I randomly see it happening to my dismay... Painting on screen by previous standards did not happen and other browsers don't do that AFAIK. You shouldn't be painting before the [list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#the-end) is done. That's goes against script spec.

I guess because so few devs understand this. Chrome seems to be trying to paint too early, and I am not happy at all about that. Chrome should not be showing anything before `interactive` or `defer` scripts are done. If this is intentional, I consider it a Chrome bug, causing cross-browser incompatibility of expectations.

And by "painting", I mean showing on screen. Painting operation in the background can happen if you like. But I don't I see any point of showing anything on screen before DOMContentLoaded occurs. That  contributes to a poor visual experience like I said.

@hexalys

> Only on Chrome AFAICT

Nope. All browsers have done it for decades. Here's a demo https://progressive-render.glitch.me.

> You shouldn't be painting before the list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing is done. That's goes against script spec.

Which spec?

> I consider it a Chrome bug

It isn't.

> But I don't I see any point of showing anything on screen before DOMContentLoaded occurs. That contributes to a poor visual experience like I said.

It vastly improves performance, as users can start reading and interacting with content before the document has loaded.

> But I don't I see any point of showing anything on screen before DOMContentLoaded occurs.

Consider this simple case:

    <body>
      Long article text here that the user wants to read.
      <script src="slow-loading-ad"></script>
    </body>

You're saying there's no point in showing the article text until that ad script at the very bottom  finishes loading.   As @jakearchibald points out there is a definite point: the user wants to read the article.

The tradeoffs might be different for applications vs documents, of course; if most of your "content" is created by async-loaded scripts as opposed to being in the HTML itself, then the situation looks quite different....

> Nope. All browsers have done it for decades.

I don't see how that url relates to my point. You do not seem to fully grasp what I am trying to explain. _Decades_ is an irrelevant characterization of the context I present. I am just speaking of the timings of `interactive` and `defer` events by HTML5 spec, which is roughly 10 years old; and my expectations per the spec definition of it and previous observed behavior for 8+ years, critically relying on `interactive`.

Again, no other desktop browser but Chrome paints anything on screen before the 'interactive' event triggers, at least until Chrome 40-50ish. I stand by and maintain that statement. I have not seen that to be the case in Firefox, Safari, IE or Edge. Please test it with my case cited below as needed on all browsers to see for yourself. But please spare me the seemingly dismissive one liners.

> Which spec?

What I already linked: [12.2.7 The end](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#the-end). I studied those fundamentals very carefully before I even started to code Javascript. I have participated in many mailing lists conversations around script loading. I have designed a extensive feature test script that simulates or fixes all event in the correct order in all browsers including serious Presto/Opera mini bugs. So I am very well versed in that subject in case you have doubts. I have used the `interactive` state as such extensively since IE8-10 (using old hacks) with this understanding in mind. And like I [said before](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/127#issuecomment-217298778), JQuery wanted to use that event for good reasons. 

> The tradeoffs might be different for applications vs documents, of course; if most of your "content" is created by async-loaded scripts as opposed to being in the HTML itself, then the situation looks quite different....

The trade-off here is unpredictable timing and browsers changing an old working behavior resulting in breakage.

> Consider this simple case:

While I understand the need to help old poorly crafted sites to load faster. In that example the user agent is making too many lose assumptions with an author's work, and can be also considered sabotaging their chosen order sequence of scripts. This can't always be a one size fits all without unintended consequences.

In that example, if the script was set a `defer` then the browser could **maybe** paint early (though I don't think so). Ultimately **a script that blocks, is a script that blocks**. My observation as a very competent author, is that Chrome is randomly (as seen on mac) or consistently (as seen on a windows) painting too early creating unintended negative consequences. It ignored that some scripts are set as such for very good (non-performance penalizing or even performance enhancing) reasons. Visually painting before it stops parsing the document is overzealous and counterproductive to me, especially considering my extensive proper use of the `interactive` event modifying the DOM purposely before it is supposed to show anything. The worse part is the inconsistency in which it happens in Chrome. Hence considering a bug.

Take a simple use case as example. Load [this page](http://www.jeffreychernin.com/) in latest Chrome. You'll see that it is likely/hopefully showing 2 buttons properly on first visual paint on the upper right corner side, as intended. Reloading the page (or navigating cached pages) changes that outcome. Chrome now arbitrarily paints one button early (just because it can, but not because it should) ignoring that there is a deliberate change of layout coming at interactive with a second Email button. Showing 2-3+ repaints with visual jumps, instead of a unique clean render, messed up my intended design.

At the moment, there is no recourse to prevent such unpredictable early live painting on screen. Other than preempting the browser with an earlier hacked event, which is undesirable. it's very discouraging when such aggressive preemptive overrides penalize well developed site with defects.

As an author I need and want a predictable timing event sequence for which I can modify the DOM with JS knowing that layout can't be painted before that. The `interactive` state was that, until Chrome 50 or so. And I object* to any said overall benefits painting pre-interactive or pre-DOMContentLoaded.

I think there needs to be a conversation for a defined standard for user agents not being allowed to paint before `interactive`, especially if events have been registered; as well as deferred scripts. Or at the very least, being able to influence such arbitrary early layouts via priority hints, up to DOMContentLoaded. Enough that any user agent shouldn't interfere with good well informed design decisions involving `interactive` and `defer`. That's a fairly simple and reasonable proposition.

How and where can we have that broader conversation?

> It vastly improves performance, as users can start reading and interacting with content before the document has loaded.

*This is an aside from my main point here. But for the sake of the argument. This is a highly debatable point for me. I partially disagree, and think that this overly aggressive proposition is a persistent misguided notion of performance at Google promoting the loading of sites that constantly repaints live on the page, instead of painting less but more meaningfully for the user to consume. I am convinced that pages would load much faster if devs were more carefully considering and using `interactive` or `defer` for critical layout components instead, focusing on clean loading content as opposed to leave it to the browser to render anything available as fast as possible, which is a tactic at best, not a loading strategy.

e.g. Between waiting 1.5 second to view a complete page, and waiting 1.25 second to see something with a 0.5 second shit-show of constant repaints with layout shifts happening right in front of my eyes. As a user, I chose the former experience as a preferable one, every time.

Google has conducted a speed perception survey without a clear conclusion that painting in bits and pieces has any major benefit from everyone's perception of performance. The readings of that survey were mixed, and there is no clear tangible conclusion to the effect of a need to paint especially **that early**.

Let me first state that I don't necessarily disagree that getting more control over first paint is useful. That's probably best discussed in a new issue.

However, as far as the HTML Standard goes there appear to be some misunderstandings. "The end" doesn't control painting, the event loop does: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#update-the-rendering. And blocking scripts only block the HTML parser, they don't block the event loop. I don't think there's anything in the HTML Standard linking these concepts the way you'd like them to be.

Demonstrating that paint does happen before everything has been parsed...

* http://web-platform-tests.live/html/obsolete/requirements-for-implementations/the-marquee-element-0/marquee-direction-down-manual.html?pipe=trickle(347:d1:1:d1:r2)
  - this renders incrementally in Firefox, Chrome, Edge. Seemingly not in Safari.
* https://html.spec.whatwg.org/
  - this paints long before everything has been parsed in at least Firefox, Chrome, Edge. (Unclear to me what Safari does.)

> However, as far as the HTML Standard goes there appear to be some misunderstandings. "The end" doesn't control painting

Nods. My reference to it is simply for the end point of parsing. Chrome stop in the middle of parsing and start painting in the middle of it indeed. I just can't make any good sense out of that...

Thanks for pointing out the event loop. Does 'rendering' mean 'paint' or 'layout' or either?
Both, basically. And parsing routinely queues tasks to update the node tree, at which point the browser could decide to render.

@hexalys I wasn't intending to be dismissive. I thought I'd provided enough evidence in a form you could verify, and no further info was needed.

I've updated it to show the document ready state at the top of the page: https://progressive-render.glitch.me/.

Can you see (like I can in Chrome, Edge, Safari and Firefox) that the `document.readyState` remains `loading`, but content is rendered on the page? Browsers have behaved like this for decades.

> At the moment, there is no recourse to prevent such unpredictable early live painting on screen.

Sure there is. At the top of your document:

```html
<style>html { display: none; }</style>
```

Then at the bottom of your document:

```html
<style>html { display: block; }</style>
```

(or change the value with JavaScript if you want to reveal the content some other time)
Here's the server code for the demo, in case it isn't clear: https://glitch.com/edit/#!/progressive-render?path=server.js

@hexalys Here's the demo running in Firefox 3 (2008): Seems like Firefox didn't support `readyState` back then, but the deferred script on that page turns the background of the page red. Since it isn't red, it's rendering before deferred scripts are executed. Here's IE8 (2009): Note that `readyState` is `interactive`, which is a bug. However, the `defer`ed script still hasn't executed.

@jakearchibald
You keep looking at it from a purely theoretical perspective ignoring my updated context... The repro use cases or exceptional cases like the long HTML spec are besides my point. I was aware of chunked transfer rendering before, or this kind of evidence. And if the UA has nothing to do and no events are coming up. Obviously it should paint, no question. 

I am speaking of a more practical sense in the context of an average page, with only a few scripts and early DOM manipulations, like my example; which validates my case of a unique Chrome exception "**in practice**".

Ask yourself. How are you suppose to insert critical dynamic content into a page if you can’t predict consistently whether the page is already shown or not? That's a non-starter for me, in the way I think about showing a page, or the way I think about the best performance and experience for my users.
What makes Chrome paint early in this case, are things I am more interested in...

The CSS display method is one hack. Thanks for mentioning! I might use that if I must. But I am hoping for a more standard long term solution. I'd be foolish to expect getting very far in convincing Chrome to change any of this in the short term.

@hexalys you made claims about the spec and implementations that have been shown to be false. I realise that can be embarrassing, especially since you made those claims so aggressively, and boasted about your experience.

You've seen the evidence. Instead of trying to find ways to dismiss it, do some more research of your own. Throttle your connection, browse the web, observe the details in dev tools. Consider that you may not be infallible.

> I was aware of chunked transfer rendering before

This has nothing to do with chunked transfer encoding.

> How are you suppose to insert critical dynamic content into a page if you can’t predict consistently whether the page is already shown or not?

The best way is to use your frontend skills to make a stable progressive render. I've written about this before: https://jakearchibald.com/2014/dont-use-flexbox-for-page-layout/.

> The CSS display method is one hack. Thanks for mentioning! I might use that if I must. But I am hoping for a more standard long term solution.

Using CSS to control the display of content isn't a hack. That's what it's made for.

> I'd be foolish to expect getting very far in convincing Chrome to change any of this in the short term.

After all these examples, in multiple browsers, over 10 years, you're still clinging to this being a recent Chrome thing?

I believe you may have an example that has changed in Chrome from your perspective (in a way that's fully spec compliant). But you cannot flip a coin once and conclude "it's always heads!", especially when others have demonstrated otherwise.

First, I’m usually wrong, so I’m sorry if I have errantly believed that the document's `readyStateChange` event (where the `readyState` is `complete`) and the window's `load` event are effectively synonymous. That’s my presupposition as you continue reading.

I received a report (in https://github.com/jonathantneal/document-promises/issues/14) that browsers are handling `complete` and `load` differently. My speculative polyfill relies on the document being `complete` rather than the window's `load` event.

The reports states that, in Safari, executing lots of code on `complete` causes it to overstep the `load` event, thus failing to execute `load` code. In Chrome, the same scenario executes `load` at a later point in time due to the code execution on `complete`.

Reviewing this PR again, I could not figure out what _should_ happen when lots of code is executed from `document.loaded`. Should it have the same effect as what was reported? Or is it just me providing a faulty implementation? Should there be guidance in this PR to reduce browser discrepancies (if there are in fact discrepancies)?

Per spec, https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html#the-end step 7 fires the two events one right after the other.  Doing stuff in the readystatechange event listeners should not affect "load" firing, apart from the listeners needing to finish running before it fires.

As far as I can tell, that's what Firefox implements.  I can't speak for other implementations...

In terms of what this PR does, it's resolving the promise right before firing the readystatechange event.  What that means in terms of when the promise handlers run depends on whether there are readystatechange listeners.  If there are, it will run after the first such listener, afaict, because that will be the next microtask checkpoint.  If there are not, it will run after the first load listener, because _that_ will be the next microtask checkpoint.  If there are no listeners for either event, they will run after this all unwinds, I think.

Maybe we want an explicit microtask checkpoint after we resolve the promise and before we fire readystatechange?
It should probably resolve after firing. I think that's the usual pattern for these kind of things.
After firing just the readystatechange, or also after firing "load"?

Sprinkling microtask checkpoints to different places would be a bit unfortunate. Breaks the generic concept of microtasks. I think we've managed to avoid that quite well. (script element execution is a special case). In my mind if one thinks there is a missing microtask checkpoint, it usually means certain tasks should be split to two pieces (and then the checkpoint would naturally happen at the end of the first task). But not sure how that applies in this case.

In this case, that would look like separate tasks for firing the "readystatechange" and "load" events or something like that.  Then other tasks could run in between those, but that might be ok.

Another option is to move the firing of "load" into the readystate change, since now we explicitly have it take different actions based on what state is being changed to, and resolve the promise after both are fired.

Yeah, I guess conceptually there could be two tasks, but those would be in a way guaranteed to run sequentially and no tasks between them, so in practice implementation could have just one task and an extra checkpoint. That is quite close to how I've been thinking script element handling.

> but those would be in a way guaranteed to run sequentially and no tasks between them

No tasks from the same task source.  Other task sources could run in between.
If they're in the same task, I'd expect to first fire all events, and then resolve any promises. We should document that pattern somewhere.

@hexalys Just wanted to point out that on Safari 12.1, I get the same issue as on Chrome (the flash of one button instead of 2 on first few paints) about 90% of the time when loading from cache but 0% of the time when loading from network (forced via dev tools), and this is identical to what I experience on Chrome. I can confirm I don't experience this issue on Firefox, however. It's not Chrome-specific, but might have to do with code common between Webkit and Blink (which started as a Webkit fork).

In either case, it's probably more appropriate to file bugs against Safari and Chrome than to discuss it here.

> If they're in the same task, I'd expect to first fire all events, and then resolve any promises. We should document that pattern somewhere.
